high-crp-what-it-means.name: High CRP: what it means and what happens next
high-crp-what-it-means.summary: A high CRP means there is inflammation or infection somewhere in the body, but not where or why, so doctors read it with symptoms and other tests.
keyPoints: A high CRP shows that inflammation or infection is likely, but it does not show where it is or what is causing it.
CRP is a protein made by the liver whose level rises when there is inflammation in the body.
Doctors read the result with the wider clinical picture, and the test is often repeated to see whether treatment has worked.
Some raised results are linked to things other than illness, such as obesity or taking the combined contraceptive pill.
Laboratories and sources do not all use the same cut-offs, so a CRP result is read against the range on its own report.

body.heading: What does a CRP test measure?
body.body:
CRP stands for C-reactive protein, a protein that the liver makes. Its level in the blood rises when there is inflammation somewhere in the body. Infection and several other causes of inflammation can push the level up.

Doctors usually request the test when they suspect an infection or inflammation, for example after surgery. It is also used to help assess long-term inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. Lab Tests Online UK says no special preparation is needed for the test.

body.heading: What does a high CRP mean?
body.body:
A high or rising CRP suggests that there is an acute infection or inflammation. It does not show where the inflammation is or which condition is causing it. For that reason the test is not diagnostic on its own. Berkshire and Surrey pathology services say a raised CRP is linked with infection, particularly but not only bacterial, and with inflammation.

A small rise is hard to interpret by itself, so doctors consider it alongside the whole clinical picture. In long-term inflammatory conditions the test is often repeated to see whether treatment is working. The cause of a high CRP cannot always be found.

body.heading: Which conditions can raise CRP?
body.body: MedlinePlus lists cancer, heart attack, infection, inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and related diseases, and rheumatic fever among the conditions that can raise CRP. Not every cause is an illness. A Danish blood donor study found low-grade inflammation was more common in women using the combined contraceptive pill. Obesity is linked with low-grade inflammation and with higher CRP levels. StatPearls describes smoking, diabetes and other long-term conditions as associated with low-grade inflammation that can raise CRP.

body.heading: What happens after a high CRP result?
body.body:
Lab Tests Online UK says CRP is used to assess how severe inflammation is and how well treatment is working. The doctor may then arrange further tests or treatment.

The test is often repeated to see whether treatment has been effective. NHS laboratories often report CRP results within about a day, though timing depends on where the test is requested. A CRP result does not show urgency; the NHS says chest tightness or pain spreading to the arms, neck or jaw needs a 999 call straight away. StatPearls notes that small CRP rises can occur without obvious widespread inflammation.

body.heading: Is hs-CRP the same test?
body.body: High-sensitivity CRP, or hs-CRP, is a separate and more sensitive version of the test. It has been used to estimate the risk of heart disease in people who seem healthy. Lab Tests Online UK notes that current UK guidelines on cardiovascular risk assessment do not recommend hs-CRP testing. A Sheffield NHS laboratory leaflet says hs-CRP should not replace assessment of the usual cardiovascular risk factors. The same leaflet says people with active infection, inflammation or trauma should not have hs-CRP testing until these have resolved. Lab Tests Online UK says recent studies suggest hs-CRP may help identify risk in healthy people, but this is not current UK practice.

body.heading: Can medicines or other factors change the result?
body.body: StatPearls states that some medicines, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and statins, can lower CRP. Long-term conditions linked with low-grade inflammation can lift it.

body.heading: Where else is CRP used?
body.body: Regional NHS guidance on suspected giant cell arteritis, an inflammation of blood vessels, asks for a CRP before steroids are started. A Devon formulary page says polymyalgia rheumatica is possible but very rare when inflammatory markers are normal. Scottish referral guidance for suspected rheumatoid arthritis refers to CRP and ESR results alongside anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor tests. It advises referral for persistent symptoms even when CRP is normal and antibodies are negative. A Scottish NHS guideline notes that a CRP level on its own does not show whether there is a bacterial infection. A Scottish NHS guideline on giant cell arteritis says it is very rare for the condition to appear with normal inflammatory markers, and that CRP, plasma viscosity or both are expected to be raised.

references.title: Lab Tests Online UK: C-reactive protein (CRP)
StatPearls: C-reactive protein, clinical relevance and interpretation

low-ferritin-what-it-means.name: Low ferritin: what it means and what next
low-ferritin-what-it-means.summary: A low ferritin level means the body's iron stores are low, and doctors then look for the cause, which is often blood loss.
keyPoints: Ferritin is a protein that stores iron, so a low level means there is not much iron in store.
Ferritin can fall before blood iron levels fall, which makes it the most useful indicator of iron deficiency.
Iron deficiency is often caused by blood loss or pregnancy, so doctors look for the source.
Inflammation, infection and liver disease can raise ferritin, so it is often read alongside CRP.
The report shows the reference range used by the laboratory, which differs between laboratories.

body.heading: What does a ferritin test measure?
body.body: Ferritin is a protein that stores iron in the body. The test estimates how much iron is held in store. Ferritin levels are low in long-term iron deficiency and high in long-term iron overload. Lab Tests Online UK describes it as the most useful indicator of iron deficiency.

body.heading: What does a low ferritin level mean?
body.body: A low ferritin points to iron deficiency. Ferritin tracks the body's iron stores, so a low result reflects low stores. Stores can drop well below normal before the iron level in the blood itself falls, so ferritin can show the problem early. Low iron can exist without anaemia, and symptoms such as tiredness can still be present. Ferritin can also fall when protein levels are very low, as in some cases of malnutrition.

body.heading: Why do iron stores run low?
body.body: The NHS says iron deficiency anaemia is caused by a lack of iron, often because of blood loss or pregnancy. NHS formulary guidance lists heavy periods, bleeding in the digestive tract, coeliac disease and a poor diet among the causes. It also lists ulcers, medicines such as aspirin and anti-inflammatory painkillers, and bowel cancer as possible digestive causes, which is why the cause is looked for. UK guidance recommends checking for coeliac disease in people with iron deficiency anaemia. An NHS leaflet says blood loss from the gut is the most common cause in adult men and postmenopausal women once other causes are excluded. Guidance says the cause of the iron deficiency matters more than the anaemia itself.

body.heading: What symptoms go with low iron?
body.body: The NHS lists tiredness, shortness of breath, noticeable heartbeats and pale skin as common symptoms. Less common symptoms include hair loss, ringing in the ears, a sore tongue and a craving for non-food items. That craving, called pica, can be for items such as ice, paper or clay. The NHS advises seeing a GP when symptoms like these appear, and a GP appointment is the usual route for a ferritin test.

body.heading: Why can a ferritin result be misleading?
body.body: Ferritin is not only a store of iron. Lab Tests Online UK says levels can be high in inflammatory conditions, infection and liver disease. Because inflammation can push ferritin up and hide a shortage of iron, CRP is often checked alongside it. A high ferritin can signal long-term iron overload, especially haemochromatosis, but further investigation is needed before that diagnosis is made. Hospital guidance notes that inflammation may raise ferritin into the normal range, which can hide iron deficiency. NHS laboratory guidance notes that ferritin thresholds vary according to the local laboratory.

body.heading: What happens next?
body.body: A GP usually takes a blood test, and ferritin is the key marker of how much iron is stored. If the cause is not clear, the GP may arrange further tests to find the source. A GP may refer to a specialist if no cause can be found. Iron tablets are the usual first treatment, and the NHS says they are taken for about six months. Side effects of iron tablets, mainly in the digestive system, are common. Iron can also be given by infusion into a vein, which is used less often. Guidance says patients are monitored in the first weeks for a haemoglobin response to iron tablets.

body.heading: What helps iron stores recover?
body.body: The NHS says iron deficiency anaemia is treated with iron tablets and with iron-rich foods. NHS guidance points to dark green leafy vegetables and dried fruit as food sources. NHS guidance says drinking orange juice after an iron tablet may help the body absorb the iron. Tea, coffee, milk and dairy foods, and wholegrain cereals can stop the body absorbing iron from other foods and tablets. One NHS page suggests taking iron tablets with or soon after food to reduce the chance of side effects. Formulary guidance says treatment continues for a period after the haemoglobin level returns to normal. Iron tablets can cause constipation, diarrhoea, tummy pain, nausea and darker stools. A normal haemoglobin does not rule out iron deficiency, because tiredness can come before haemoglobin falls. Iron given into a vein is considered when tablets have not worked or a rapid rise in iron is needed. A Scottish guideline notes that pregnant women lose iron during and after delivery. It recommends that women who start oral iron continue it through pregnancy and for some months after the birth. An NHS leaflet says anaemia in pregnancy and after birth is very common and is usually treated with tablets.

references.title: Lab Tests Online UK: Ferritin test

cholesterol-blood-test-results-explained.name: Cholesterol test results explained
cholesterol-blood-test-results-explained.summary: A cholesterol test reports total, HDL and non-HDL cholesterol plus triglycerides, and doctors read them with other risk factors.
keyPoints: A standard cholesterol test reports total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and non-HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides are usually measured with them.
Non-HDL cholesterol is total cholesterol minus HDL, and it covers all the harmful types together.
Doctors use cholesterol results with age, blood pressure and health conditions to estimate the risk of cardiovascular disease.
Where treatment is needed, guidance recommends lifestyle support and often a statin, with the test repeated afterwards.

body.heading: What does a cholesterol blood test measure?
body.body: A lipid profile measures lipids in the blood, such as cholesterol and triglycerides. The sample is taken from a vein in the arm, sometimes after fasting. A standard test reports total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and non-HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides are usually measured alongside them. NHS laboratories usually calculate LDL cholesterol from total cholesterol, HDL and triglycerides rather than measuring it directly. Total cholesterol is the combined figure, covering both good and bad cholesterol together. NICE guidance dropped routine fasting for a lipid profile, according to one NHS laboratory.

body.heading: What do HDL, non-HDL and triglycerides mean?
body.body: HDL is generally treated as the protective part of the total, and a low HDL counts as a risk marker. Non-HDL cholesterol is total cholesterol minus HDL. It captures the combined harmful types of cholesterol, and some NHS laboratories prefer it to LDL when samples are not fasting. Lab Tests Online UK notes that non-HDL does not need a fasting sample, which makes it practical. Triglycerides are a type of fat in the blood. Fasting is no longer routinely required, though some laboratories ask for a fasting repeat when a non-fasting triglyceride result is very high. The BHF gives healthy cholesterol targets and says the goal is lower after a heart attack or stroke. Sources differ slightly on where they place the line for triglycerides, and laboratories differ in their reference ranges. For that reason the laboratory report shows the range used for each result.

body.heading: How does a doctor use the result?
body.body: Doctors use the cholesterol result with age, blood pressure and health conditions to estimate the risk of cardiovascular disease. The QRISK tool estimates cardiovascular risk and helps decide whether treatment is needed. For people who already have cardiovascular disease, pathways move to secondary prevention, which does not use QRISK. People can ask their GP, or may be offered a test at a pharmacy or through an NHS Health Check in England.

body.heading: What helps lower raised cholesterol?
body.body: People at higher risk are offered support with lifestyle changes such as diet, exercise, stopping smoking and managing weight. In primary prevention, lifestyle support is given for a few months before the level is reassessed. Pathways list atorvastatin as the usual first statin for primary prevention, with a higher starting dose for people who already have cardiovascular disease. Ezetimibe is a second-line option if the aim is not reached. Someone who has side effects on a high-intensity statin can be offered a lower dose or another statin. The test is repeated after treatment starts to see whether the level has fallen.

body.heading: Why does raised cholesterol matter?
body.body: The BHF explains that extra cholesterol can build up as fatty material in the arteries and narrow them. That gradual build-up raises the risk of heart attack and stroke. Having more risk factors, such as smoking or high blood pressure, raises the overall risk further. Most people with high cholesterol have no symptoms. The BHF lists lumps on the tendons, yellow lumps around the eyelids and a pale ring around the iris as possible signs, though many people have none.

body.heading: What is familial hypercholesterolaemia?
body.body: Familial hypercholesterolaemia is an inherited form of high cholesterol. In familial hypercholesterolaemia the high cholesterol is usually present from birth. The BHF says a heart attack or stroke at a younger age, or relatives with early heart disease, can point to it. The BHF says that if one parent has familial hypercholesterolaemia, a child has a 1 in 2 chance of also having it.

body.heading: What do statins do, and who is offered them?
body.body: NHS guidance says statins may be offered to people at higher risk of cardiovascular disease when healthy lifestyle changes have not helped or are unlikely to help on their own. They are also used in people who already have heart disease and in people with inherited high cholesterol. If statins are unsuitable, other cholesterol-lowering medicines can be offered. Targets may be lower for people with conditions such as diabetes or cardiovascular disease, according to NHS 111 Wales. The NHS says some people should not take statins, including those with severe liver disease and those who are pregnant or trying to conceive. The NHS says higher risk can be shown by a QRISK assessment, by conditions such as diabetes, chronic kidney disease or familial hypercholesterolaemia, or by being aged 85 or over. The BHF says most people have no side effects from statins.

hba1c-test-what-it-shows.name: HbA1c test: what it shows and why it matters
hba1c-test-what-it-shows.summary: The HbA1c test shows average blood glucose over the past two to three months and is used to diagnose and monitor diabetes.
keyPoints: HbA1c reflects the average blood glucose level over roughly the previous two to three months.
The test is used to diagnose diabetes, to check how well diabetes is managed and to follow people with prediabetes.
Targets are personal, and a diabetes team may set a higher one for someone with frequent low blood glucose or an older person.
Conditions that affect red blood cells can make HbA1c unreliable, and another test may suit better.

body.heading: What does an HbA1c test show?
body.body: The HbA1c blood test reflects the average level of glucose in the blood over the past two to three months. That is why it differs from a finger-prick reading, which captures one moment. Glucose attaches to a part of the red blood cell, and the more glucose there is in the blood, the more HbA1c is present. Red blood cells live for about two to three months before new ones replace them, which sets the window the test covers. Because it covers a longer window, the test does not show short-term rises or dips in glucose.

body.heading: What is the test used for?
body.body: Doctors use it to diagnose diabetes. They also use it to keep an eye on levels in people at risk of developing diabetes, a state called prediabetes. In people who already have diabetes, it shows how well blood sugar has been controlled. MedlinePlus says the test is not used to diagnose type 1 diabetes. Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed with blood tests, and HbA1c is the usual first test. HbA1c is not used to diagnose diabetes during pregnancy.

body.heading: How are the results given and what are the targets?
body.body: UK laboratories give HbA1c in millimoles per mole, while some countries use a percentage. NICE-based guidance says an individual HbA1c target should be agreed with each person. A higher target may suit someone who has had many problems with low blood glucose. As people age, the diabetes team may raise the target, because the risks of tight control can outweigh the benefits.

body.heading: How often is it done?
body.body: NICE patient information advises that HbA1c is usually tested every three to six months. It may be done more often if blood glucose levels are changing quickly. Once blood glucose is stable, NICE patient information says the test is usually every six months.

body.heading: What can make the result less reliable?
body.body: Conditions that affect red blood cells can make the result less accurate, such as anaemia or an uncommon form of haemoglobin. Where HbA1c is unreliable, glucose-based blood tests are used for diagnosis instead. Pregnancy, heavy bleeding and recent blood transfusion can also make HbA1c unreliable. An NHS Scotland resource says the HbA1c may change if diet, physical activity, weight or medication have changed. An estimated average glucose converts HbA1c into meter units, but it is an average and not an exact match for readings. One hospital guideline says HbA1c should not be used for diagnosis when symptoms have appeared over less than a month. Heavy bleeding or haemolytic anaemia can make HbA1c falsely low, while iron deficiency may raise it. Some haemoglobin variants can interfere with HbA1c measurement, so other methods may be needed.

body.heading: What happens after a result in the prediabetes range?
body.body: The usual response to an intermediate result is lifestyle advice on eating, activity and weight. A GP can refer eligible people to the free NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme, and some areas allow self-referral. People with an intermediate result are usually monitored at least once a year. A GP appointment is the route to discuss any result. A raised result in someone without symptoms is usually repeated, and a second result in the diabetes range confirms the diagnosis. Eligibility for the Diabetes Prevention Programme varies by area, so the local service sets the rules.

body.heading: Why does a prediabetes result matter?
body.body: Prediabetes means blood sugar is higher than normal but not high enough for a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. It also means a high risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Prediabetes usually causes no symptoms, so it is found through blood tests. Feeling very thirsty, passing urine more often, feeling more tired than usual and losing weight without trying are symptoms of diabetes itself. The NHS notes that not everyone with diabetes has symptoms, which is why getting checked matters. The programme is free, lasts nine months and gives support with healthy eating, physical activity and weight.

liver-function-tests-what-results-mean.name: Liver blood tests: what the results mean
liver-function-tests-what-results-mean.summary: Liver blood tests can point towards a possible problem but do not name the cause, and results that are not normal are very common.
keyPoints: Liver blood tests, once called liver function tests, are a group of tests that can include ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin.
A result outside the reference range does not always mean liver disease, and a normal result does not always rule it out.
The pattern of results helps point towards liver cell injury or a problem with bile flow.
Yellowing of the skin or eyes needs an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111, according to the NHS.

body.heading: What are liver blood tests?
body.body: Liver blood tests are a group of blood tests, once known as liver function tests or LFTs. They can include ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin.

body.heading: What do ALT and AST show?
body.body: ALT and AST are enzymes that leak into the blood when liver cells are injured. ALT is more specific to the liver, while AST can also be high when muscle is damaged elsewhere in the body. Common causes of this pattern include viral hepatitis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, alcohol-related liver disease, autoimmune hepatitis and drug-induced liver injury. In alcohol-related liver injury AST is often higher than ALT, whereas in fatty liver disease ALT is often the higher of the two. Muscle injury, a heart attack and an underactive thyroid can also raise ALT and AST.

body.heading: What do ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin show?
body.body: Raised ALP and GGT point towards a problem with the flow of bile. Causes include blocked bile ducts, for example by stones, and some long-term diseases of the bile ducts. ALP also comes from bone, so GGT helps to show whether the liver is the source. Raised bilirubin causes jaundice, a yellowing of the eyes and skin. Bilirubin can also be raised without liver disease, as in Gilbert's syndrome, where the other liver tests are normal. Albumin is affected only when liver disease is at a severe stage, and other factors can also change albumin results. A normal GGT alongside a raised ALP points towards a source other than the liver, such as bone. Bilirubin is a pigment made when red blood cells break down, and the liver normally clears it. Albumin is a protein made by the liver.

body.heading: Does an abnormal result mean liver disease?
body.body: Abnormal results can occur in conditions that do not involve the liver, and normal results can be found in people with serious liver disease. The British Liver Trust says it is very common to have some liver blood test results that are not normal. It also says it is possible to have a normal liver blood test result and still have a serious liver condition. Medicines and herbal supplements can raise liver enzymes, as can some non-liver problems such as muscle injury. Guidelines usually start by repeating the tests, and move to further checks if results stay abnormal.

body.heading: What happens after an abnormal result?
body.body: Laboratories compare each result with their own range, so results are compared only with the range of the laboratory that did the test. If the results suggest a liver problem, a GP may calculate a FIB-4 index, which gives an indication of the amount of scarring in the liver. Depending on the results, age and possible causes, a GP may arrange more tests or regular repeat tests. Further tests can look for the cause, such as viral hepatitis, fatty liver disease or an effect of alcohol or medicines. Pathways differ between areas on when to repeat tests and which scores trigger referral, so the steps a GP follows can vary.

body.heading: When is yellowing of the skin urgent?
body.body: The NHS says jaundice can be a sign of something serious such as liver disease. It advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111 when the skin or whites of the eyes look yellow. On brown or black skin the yellow colour is easier to see in the whites of the eyes. Itchy skin, darker urine and paler stools can come with it.

body.heading: What are fatty liver and alcohol-related liver disease?
body.body: NHS guidance names non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, in some pathways now called MASLD, as a common cause of abnormal liver tests. NHS hospital guidance says fatty liver disease (MASLD) is treated mainly by reversing its underlying cause, with weight loss a key part. Where alcohol is the cause, one pathway advises cutting out alcohol and repeating the test after a month. Local guidance suggests repeating the tests, including after stopping a medicine that may be affecting the liver. If results stay abnormal, guidance supports an ultrasound scan of the liver and bile ducts and blood tests for viral and autoimmune causes. Local pathways use a FibroScan result, as well as FIB-4, to decide who is referred to a liver clinic. Common causes of jaundice include alcohol-related liver disease, gallstones, hepatitis, pancreatitis and sickle cell disease.

egfr-and-creatinine-kidney-blood-tests.name: eGFR and creatinine: kidney test results
egfr-and-creatinine-kidney-blood-tests.summary: Creatinine and eGFR show how well the kidneys filter blood, and kidney disease is confirmed only when abnormal results persist.
keyPoints: Creatinine is a waste product measured in the blood, and eGFR is an estimate of kidney filtering worked out from it.
As kidney function declines, the eGFR may fall over time.
One abnormal result is not enough to diagnose chronic kidney disease, which is confirmed when eGFR stays low over about three months.
A urine test, the albumin to creatinine ratio, is used alongside eGFR because it can show kidney damage.

body.heading: What are creatinine and eGFR?
body.body: Creatinine is a waste product, and the blood test measures how much of it is in the blood. The eGFR, or estimated glomerular filtration rate, is calculated from the creatinine result. The calculation also takes account of age and sex. Lab Tests Online UK explains that the eGFR may fall over time as kidney function declines. Because eGFR comes from a routine blood test, it lets clinicians spot kidney problems before symptoms appear. UK laboratories report an eGFR alongside every creatinine result, in line with NICE guidance. People with more muscle naturally make more creatinine, which can give a lower eGFR than their kidney function really is. Cystatin C is another marker filtered by the kidneys and is less affected by muscle mass than creatinine.

body.heading: What does a low eGFR mean?
body.body: A low eGFR may be a sign of kidney disease, though a single result is not enough to say. NICE says testing for chronic kidney disease uses both an eGFR and a urine ACR. A slightly raised urine ACR, which checks for the protein albumin, may indicate early-stage kidney disease. eGFR falls naturally with age, which does not always mean kidney disease. The estimate is unreliable when kidney function is changing quickly, as in acute kidney injury.

body.heading: How is chronic kidney disease confirmed?
body.body: One abnormal result is not enough. A diagnosis is usually confirmed only if repeated eGFR tests are consistently lower than normal over about three months. NICE says a low first eGFR should be repeated soon, to check whether sudden kidney injury is the cause. The urine albumin to creatinine ratio, or ACR, compares albumin with creatinine in a urine sample. Alongside the eGFR, urine tests give a more accurate picture of how well the kidneys are working. Results are classed by eGFR category and by ACR category, which together show the stage. The NHS says a very low ACR usually means the kidneys are working normally, while a very high one points to more severe kidney disease.

body.heading: Who is tested?
body.body: Testing is recommended for people with risk factors such as diabetes, high blood pressure, past acute kidney injury or cardiovascular disease. Early chronic kidney disease often causes no symptoms, so it is commonly found through routine blood or urine tests. Later symptoms can include tiredness, swollen ankles, feet or hands, shortness of breath, blood in the urine and passing urine more often at night. The NHS advises seeing a GP about symptoms that persist. NHS 111 Wales lists kidney stones, lupus and a family history of advanced or inherited kidney disease among the risk factors.

body.heading: What are the limits of the test?
body.body: Creatinine-based eGFR may be less reliable in older adults. In that situation another marker, cystatin C, can help. Creatinine can also be influenced by factors other than the kidneys, such as how much muscle a person has. NICE advises that the urine ACR is ideally measured on an early morning sample.

body.heading: What happens after a diagnosis?
body.body: Chronic kidney disease is most often caused by damage from other conditions, most commonly diabetes and high blood pressure. There is no cure, but care can slow progression. Kidney function is monitored with regular blood and urine tests. Care centres on blood pressure control, managing diabetes, prescribed medicines, diet advice and not smoking. The NHS says medicines can help control related problems and keep the kidneys working for longer. The NHS says most people with chronic kidney disease can control the condition with medicine and regular check-ups. Glomerulonephritis, inflammation of the filters inside the kidneys, is another cause of kidney disease.

body.heading: How often are kidney tests repeated?
body.body: NICE guideline NG203 says the monitoring frequency it recommends is a minimum, and that more frequent monitoring may suit some people. NICE sets a minimum number of checks each year, which depends on the eGFR and ACR categories. It also reflects how quickly the eGFR or ACR is changing and other conditions such as diabetes. NICE says ACR monitoring should be individualised, for example more often when the ACR is higher. NICE lists diabetes among the risk factors for which eGFR and ACR testing is advised.

high-white-blood-cell-count-causes.name: High white blood cell count: what it means
high-white-blood-cell-count-causes.summary: A high white blood cell count is a non-specific sign, most often from infection, and doctors read it with the type of cell raised.
keyPoints: A high white cell count can be caused by infection, inflammation, some medicines, stress or smoking, and less often by a blood disorder.
The differential count shows which type of white cell is raised, which helps narrow down the cause.
A mild, lasting rise is often linked to chronic inflammation, infection or smoking, while an unexplained very high count leads to urgent referral to haematology.
A single high count does not diagnose anything, and doctors may repeat the test.

body.heading: What does the full blood count measure?
body.body: A full blood count measures the number and type of cells in the blood, including red cells, white cells and platelets. The test gives a total white cell count and a differential that splits white cells into types. Those types include neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils. Neutrophils are the main defence against bacterial infection.

body.heading: What does a high white cell count mean?
body.body: A raised count is a non-specific signal, which means it does not point to one cause. A high count can indicate infection, inflammation, or leukaemia and other blood disorders. Infection, most often bacterial infection, is the most common cause. Results vary with age and time of day, and older people sometimes do not show a raised count even when they have an infection.

body.heading: What else can raise it?
body.body: Inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis can raise the count, and so can allergies. Some medicines, for example corticosteroids, can raise it. Physical or emotional stress can affect the white cell count. Smoking and pregnancy can also raise the count. Corticosteroids raise the white cell count partly by increasing the release of neutrophils from the bone marrow. Physical stress can make the white cell count rise within hours, because the body holds a large store of neutrophils in the bone marrow and blood vessels.

body.heading: What does the differential add?
body.body: A high neutrophil count usually suggests bacterial infection, inflammation or physical stress on the body. A high lymphocyte count can occur with viral infections or with conditions such as chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. Leukaemia and Hodgkin disease are among the conditions that can cause a high white cell count. Reactive lymphocytes on a blood film point to infection, typically viral, as the likely cause of a raised lymphocyte count. Smoking commonly causes a mild rise in neutrophils, lymphocytes or both.

body.heading: What happens next?
body.body: A hospital guideline from Hampshire says a mild, lasting rise is likely to come from a chronic inflammatory or infective process, or from smoking. The same guideline says an unexplained, very high count prompts an urgent referral to haematology. Doctors read the count with symptoms, the differential and sometimes a repeat test or a blood film. Reference ranges differ with age, sex and laboratory, so the report shows the range used. The NHS says severe breathing difficulty, or someone who has passed out and is not responding normally, needs a 999 call. Medicines and a recent blood transfusion can also change white cell results, according to laboratory guidance.

body.heading: When might a blood disorder be considered?
body.body: A GP may arrange a blood test if leukaemia is suspected, and a very high white cell count could be a sign of it. In that case the person is referred urgently to a specialist in blood conditions, called a haematologist. UK sources list tiredness, bleeding or bruising easily, night sweats, weight loss and frequent infections among leukaemia symptoms. Cancer Research UK says leukaemia symptoms can be vague, and that minor conditions are common while leukaemia is rare. For chronic myeloid leukaemia the NHS advises a non-urgent GP visit if symptoms appear. For suspected leukaemia the NHS says a GP asks about symptoms and medical history, examines the person and sends a blood sample for testing.

thyroid-blood-tests-tsh-and-t4-explained.name: Thyroid blood tests: TSH and T4 explained
thyroid-blood-tests-tsh-and-t4-explained.summary: Thyroid tests read TSH and free T4 together, because free T4 helps to interpret an abnormal TSH.
keyPoints: TSH is the main test for thyroid problems, and free T4 helps to interpret an abnormal TSH.
Free T4 is measured when the TSH is raised, to tell overt from subclinical hypothyroidism.
A slightly raised TSH with a normal free T4 is called subclinical hypothyroidism and is followed over time.
Severe illness and some medicines can change thyroid results without a thyroid disease.

body.heading: What do TSH and T4 show?
body.body: The thyroid is a gland in the neck that makes thyroid hormones. TSH is linked to the pituitary gland, and a pituitary problem can cause too much or too little of it. A medical review describes TSH as the main test for finding problems with the thyroid gland itself. Free T4 is measured to tell overt from subclinical hypothyroidism when the TSH is raised. Results are read as a pattern of TSH and free T4 together, not one number alone.

body.heading: What pattern suggests an underactive thyroid?
body.body: A high TSH with a low free T4 suggests an underactive thyroid, called hypothyroidism. The NHS says an underactive thyroid is diagnosed with blood tests for TSH and T4. The NHS says diagnosis of an underactive thyroid also usually involves a neck examination. Thyroid UK says some people continue to have symptoms while taking levothyroxine.

body.heading: What pattern suggests an overactive thyroid?
body.body: A British Thyroid Foundation leaflet says an overactive thyroid, or hyperthyroidism, is diagnosed with a blood test measuring thyroid hormones.

body.heading: What if the results are borderline?
body.body: A slightly raised TSH with a normal free T4 is called subclinical hypothyroidism. The British Thyroid Foundation says blood TSH levels return to normal in around half of people with subclinical thyroid disease. A test for thyroid antibodies helps to judge that risk. The British Thyroid Foundation says there is little clinical evidence that treatment gives long-term benefit in subclinical thyroid disease. MedlinePlus says abnormal T4 levels can sometimes be a sign of a pituitary problem that causes too much or too little TSH. A raised TSH with a normal free T4 is often repeated after about three months, because it can be a temporary finding.

body.heading: Can illness or medicines change the result?
body.body: Abnormal T4 levels do not always mean a condition that needs treatment. MedlinePlus says pregnancy, oestrogen levels, liver problems and severe body-wide illness can affect T4 results.

body.heading: What happens after a diagnosis?
body.body: Underactive thyroid is usually treated with daily hormone replacement tablets called levothyroxine. The NHS says this treatment is long term to prevent symptoms. NHS inform says a mild case with no symptoms may not need treatment. Regular blood tests check the dose is right, and NHS inform says side effects usually only occur with too much levothyroxine. Thyroid UK says that if symptoms do not improve on levothyroxine, TSH is measured again and the dose may be adjusted. Pregnancy often means the levothyroxine dose needs to be changed, according to the NHS.

body.heading: What can cause an underactive or overactive thyroid?
body.body: In the UK the main cause of an underactive thyroid is an autoimmune condition called Hashimoto's disease. Symptoms of an underactive thyroid tend to appear gradually and can be mild, such as tiredness, weight gain, constipation and low mood. Graves' disease is the most common cause of an overactive thyroid. Symptoms of an overactive thyroid include nervousness, poor sleep, a fast or irregular heartbeat, trembling and weight loss. Treatment for an overactive thyroid can include anti-thyroid medicines, beta-blockers for symptoms such as tremor, and radioactive iodine. Radioactive iodine often leads to an underactive thyroid afterwards. TSH receptor antibodies are associated with Graves' disease, so antibody tests can help find the cause of an overactive thyroid. People with a family history of thyroid problems are more likely to develop an underactive thyroid, the NHS says. Some people with Graves' disease develop eye problems, known as thyroid eye disease. Thyroid eye disease may get worse after radioactive iodine, so doctors discuss this beforehand. Beta-blockers ease symptoms in the first weeks of an overactive thyroid but do not change how much hormone the thyroid makes.

vitamin-b12-and-folate-tests-explained.name: Vitamin B12 and folate tests explained
vitamin-b12-and-folate-tests-explained.summary: Blood tests for B12 and folate help diagnose deficiency, but a B12 test can miss cases, so symptoms matter too.
keyPoints: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency can both cause anaemia in which the body makes abnormally large red blood cells.
A GP combines symptoms with blood tests that check the level of vitamin B12 and of folate.
A UK clinical guideline says a B12 blood test is not completely reliable, so two tests are requested when deficiency is suspected.
B12 deficiency is usually treated with injections of hydroxocobalamin, and folate deficiency with folic acid tablets.

body.heading: What are vitamin B12 and folate deficiency anaemia?
body.body: Vitamin B12 and folate are both needed to make healthy red blood cells. When either is lacking, the body can make abnormally large red blood cells that do not work as they should. This is called vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia. Some problems caused by B12 or folate deficiency can be irreversible if left untreated. Folate deficiency can affect fertility, though this is usually temporary and can be reversed with folate supplements. The NHS says B12 and folate deficiency are both more common in older people. Folate deficiency is caused mainly by poor diet, pregnancy, or drugs that interfere with folate. A UK prescribing guideline lists green vegetables, beans and pulses and citrus fruit as rich sources of folate. A blood test for intrinsic factor antibodies helps diagnose pernicious anaemia. For borderline B12 results, local guidance recommends methylmalonic acid or homocysteine tests to check for functional deficiency.

body.heading: What symptoms can it cause?
body.body: The NHS lists tiredness, muscle weakness, numbness, pins and needles, psychological problems and problems with balance and coordination. Breathlessness, headaches, palpitations and pale or yellowish skin also appear in some lists of symptoms. A Glasgow-area hospital note says nerve effects of B12 deficiency can occur without anaemia. Mouth ulcers, a sore red tongue and problems with vision or memory are also listed. The NHS says folic acid is usually taken for about four months, and for longer if the cause continues.

body.heading: How is it diagnosed?
body.body: A GP typically combines symptoms with blood tests. The blood tests check the level of vitamin B12 and the level of folate in the blood. A UK clinical guideline notes that a vitamin B12 blood test is not completely reliable and asks for two tests when deficiency is suspected. An NHS haematology service says B12 testing should be limited to people with suspected deficiency and not used as a screening test. Guidance advises referral to a haematologist when the cause of deficiency is still uncertain after investigation.

body.heading: What causes deficiency?
body.body: The NHS says pernicious anaemia is the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency in the UK. Pernicious anaemia is an autoimmune condition that affects the stomach, so B12 from food is not absorbed. Lack of B12 from the diet is uncommon, but it can happen with a vegan diet that includes no supplements or fortified foods. Some medicines, including proton pump inhibitors and metformin, can reduce B12 levels. The NHS notes that some medicines, including anticonvulsants, can affect how much of these vitamins the body absorbs.

body.heading: How is it treated?
body.body: B12 deficiency anaemia is usually treated with injections of vitamin B12, called hydroxocobalamin. When the cause is diet, treatment may be daily B12 tablets instead. Folate deficiency is usually treated with folic acid tablets. Clinicians check B12 status first, because folic acid can mask a vitamin B12 deficiency. Follow-up blood tests check that treatment is working. A GP appointment is the route for symptoms such as numbness, pins and needles or problems with balance.

vitamin-d-blood-test-who-needs-one.name: Vitamin D blood test: who needs one?
vitamin-d-blood-test-who-needs-one.summary: NHS guidance does not recommend routine vitamin D tests for people without symptoms, and testing is kept for specific symptoms or conditions.
keyPoints: NHS guidance says not to test routinely for vitamin D deficiency in people without symptoms.
Testing is considered for bone pain, muscle weakness, or abnormal calcium, phosphate or parathyroid hormone results.
A lack of vitamin D can cause rickets in children and bone pain from osteomalacia in adults.
The NHS says everyone can consider a daily supplement in autumn and winter, and people at higher risk all year.

body.heading: What does a vitamin D blood test show?
body.body: The test measures the level of vitamin D in the blood, usually as 25-hydroxyvitamin D. The body makes vitamin D under the skin when it is exposed to sunlight. In the UK, the sun is too low in the sky for the skin to make vitamin D from about October to early March. The routine test measures 25-hydroxyvitamin D because it is the best marker of overall vitamin D status and stays in the blood longer than the active form. The liver makes 25-hydroxyvitamin D first, and the kidneys then convert it into the fully active form.

body.heading: Who is tested and who is not?
body.body: NHS guidance says not to test routinely for vitamin D deficiency in people without symptoms. Testing is generally considered for bone pain or softness in adults, a condition called osteomalacia, and for unexplained muscle weakness. It is also considered after abnormal calcium, phosphate or parathyroid hormone results, and before some bone treatments. People at higher risk who have no symptoms do not need routine testing but should be advised on a maintenance supplement. Higher risk applies to people over a certain age, those who get little sun and those with darker skin.

body.heading: What does a low level cause?
body.body: A lack of vitamin D can cause rickets in children. In adults it can cause bone pain through osteomalacia. Some people notice tiredness or general aches and pains, which are easy to put down to other causes. In some cases the bones can become softer. One NHS policy says the evidence linking low vitamin D to conditions other than bone health is inconsistent or absent.

body.heading: How are the results read?
body.body: Lab Tests Online UK describes results as deficient, possibly inadequate for some people, or sufficient for almost everyone. In the middle band, one NHS guideline says treatment may be appropriate for some patients. Local guidance varies, so the report shows the range used by the laboratory. A doctor interprets the result in the context of symptoms, bone health and any risk factors. One NHS formulary says re-testing is generally left until at least three months after treatment starts.

body.heading: Who is advised to take a supplement?
body.body: UK public health guidance advises that everyone should consider a daily vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter. Scottish advice is similar and applies from age five upwards. People at higher risk are advised to take a supplement all year, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, children under five, and people with little sun exposure. People of African, African-Caribbean and South Asian origin are also in the higher-risk group. Clinical guidance warns that very high doses of vitamin D can be toxic and raise blood calcium. Local NHS guidance generally says supplements for prevention should be bought over the counter, with prescribing kept for diagnosed deficiency. Children under five are advised to take vitamin drops containing vitamin D all year. People aged 65 and over, and those who are housebound or live in care homes, are also considered at higher risk.

body.heading: Where else does vitamin D come from?
body.body: Sunlight on the skin is the main source in the warmer months. Few foods contain much vitamin D, so food alone is usually not enough.

body.heading: What are rickets and osteomalacia?
body.body: Low vitamin D often causes no symptoms. Some people have symptoms such as tiredness and aches. Rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults are described as the best understood consequences of vitamin D deficiency. Darker skin and covering most of the body with clothing are recognised risk factors for vitamin D deficiency. Low levels can reflect limited sun exposure, low dietary intake or a problem absorbing vitamin D from the gut.

troponin-blood-test-what-it-shows.name: Troponin blood test: what it shows
troponin-blood-test-what-it-shows.summary: A troponin test measures proteins released when heart muscle is damaged, and a raised result does not always mean a heart attack.
keyPoints: Troponin T and troponin I are proteins released into the blood when heart muscle is damaged.
The more damage, the more troponin reaches the blood, and levels rise over hours, so the test is often repeated.
A raised troponin may point to a heart attack, but other conditions can raise it too.
The NHS says to call 999 for chest pain that is tight or squeezing, or that spreads to the arms, neck or jaw.

body.heading: What is troponin?
body.body: Troponin T and troponin I are proteins found in heart muscle. They are released into the blood when the heart muscle is damaged, for example in a heart attack. The more damage there is, the more troponin reaches the blood. The NHS says troponin is the protein doctors most commonly measure in blood tests for heart damage.

body.heading: Why is a troponin test done?
body.body: Clinicians mainly use the test to check whether a heart attack is happening or has recently happened. It is typically ordered when someone has chest pain or other signs of a heart attack. An NHS laboratory describes troponin as also helping to predict short-term and longer-term outcomes in acute coronary syndrome.

body.heading: How is it used in hospital?
body.body: The NHS treats an ECG as an important early test in a suspected heart attack, and says it should be done within 10 minutes of arrival at hospital. Blood tests look for troponin, which leaks slowly into the blood after damage to the heart. Levels usually rise over hours, so testing is often repeated over several hours. NICE describes taking a second troponin sample after the first, with timing that depends on the test and the first result. High-sensitivity tests can detect much smaller amounts of troponin than older tests.

body.heading: What does a normal or raised result mean?
body.body: MedlinePlus says normal levels hours after symptoms start make a heart attack unlikely, but doctors read results alongside symptoms and the ECG. Very high levels most often mean a heart attack has occurred. Raised levels do not always mean a heart attack, because other heart conditions can raise troponin. A UK study reported by University Hospital Southampton found raised troponin in some people with unrelated conditions, so results need careful interpretation. After a heart attack, levels may stay high for one to two weeks. MedlinePlus lists conditions such as an abnormally fast heartbeat, pulmonary hypertension and congestive heart failure as other causes of a raised level. MedlinePlus says a single normal result may be followed by a retest, and a high result usually leads to two or more tests over 24 hours. A Scottish NHS guide says troponin T can stay raised in people with kidney problems or heart failure, so doctors look for a change between samples. The Southampton study's lead suggested that the normal cut-off, set using fairly healthy people, may not suit a general hospital population.

body.heading: How do the results fit with the ECG?
body.body: The ECG and troponin results together help to identify the type of heart attack. A STEMI shows particular changes on the ECG. An NSTEMI is found when the ECG does not show those changes but blood tests show heart damage. The NHS says an ECG is painless and takes about 5 minutes. NICE says a STEMI can usually be diagnosed by ECG alone, without waiting for a blood test.

body.heading: When is chest pain an emergency?
body.body: The NHS advises calling 999 for chest pain that feels tight or squeezing, or that spreads to the arms, neck or jaw. The NHS also advises calling 999 for someone who has passed out. The BHF advises calling an ambulance rather than travelling to hospital yourself, because paramedics can start care and tests on the way. The BHF says paramedics can start care and tests, including an ECG, on the way to hospital.

body.heading: What do NICE recommendations say about newer tests?
body.body: NICE recommends high-sensitivity troponin tests as options for ruling out a type of heart attack called NSTEMI in emergency departments. NICE describes strategies using a single sample on arrival or a second sample after the first, depending on the test and result. A review notes that troponin levels tend to be lower in women than in men because of smaller heart size.

inr-blood-test-warfarin-explained.name: INR blood test and warfarin explained
inr-blood-test-warfarin-explained.summary: The INR blood test shows how long blood takes to clot, and it is how the effect of warfarin is monitored so the dose can be adjusted.
keyPoints: The INR measures how long the blood takes to clot, and it is the main way warfarin treatment is monitored.
Warfarin has no fixed dose, so the dose is adjusted from INR results by an anticoagulation clinic.
New medicines, alcohol and diet can change the INR.
The main side effect of warfarin is bleeding; NHS leaflets advise a GP or NHS 111 for minor bleeding and 999 if it will not stop.

body.heading: What does the INR measure?
body.body: INR stands for international normalised ratio. It is a standard blood test that measures how long the blood takes to clot. One NHS trust explains that it compares the clotting time of a person taking warfarin with that of someone who is not.

body.heading: Why is the INR checked on warfarin?
body.body: Warfarin does not have a fixed dose. The dose needed depends on how much the medicine slows the clotting of the blood, and the INR test measures that effect. The main side effect of warfarin is an increased risk of bleeding. One NHS trust explains that an INR of 2.0 means the blood takes roughly twice as long to clot as it would without warfarin. The target INR depends on the reason for treatment, and the consultant sets the exact target.

body.heading: How often is it done?
body.body: At the start, testing is frequent. Once the result is stable, the gaps between tests lengthen. Some people need tests more regularly than others. The INR results go to the warfarin clinic, which advises on the ongoing dose and the date of the next test. One NHS trust says that once the INR is stable, the gap between blood tests can lengthen to as much as 8 to 12 weeks.

body.heading: What can change the INR?
body.body: New medicines can change the effect of warfarin, so one NHS service asks for an INR test soon after any new medicine is started or stopped. Alcohol, diet and other medicines can also move the result. Sources name cranberry and grapefruit juice as drinks to avoid on warfarin, and binge drinking as able to raise the INR. They also name ibuprofen and similar painkillers as able to increase the risk of bleeding. The NHS advises telling the GP, anticoagulant clinic or pharmacist about any prescription, over-the-counter or herbal medicine, including aspirin and St John's wort. NHS advice is that people taking warfarin should never binge drink.

body.heading: What should people know about bleeding?
body.body: Signs of bleeding include bleeding gums, blood in vomit, blood in urine or stool, and prolonged bleeding from small cuts. For women, heavier periods can be a sign. NHS trust leaflets say to contact the GP or NHS 111 about minor bruising or bleeding. NHS leaflets say to call 999 if bleeding cannot be stopped. NHS trust leaflets list vomiting or coughing up blood as a reason to seek care at A&E. NHS guidance says a significant blow to the head is a reason to call 999.

body.heading: What else do people on warfarin carry or watch?
body.body: People on warfarin are given an anticoagulant alert card to carry. The card lets medical staff identify that someone takes warfarin if there is an accident. Foods high in vitamin K, such as leafy green vegetables, can affect how warfarin works. Dietary advice from an NHS trust stresses eating a steady amount of such foods, because the clinic adjusts the dose to match. The NHS says the food and drink restrictions do not usually apply to the newer anticoagulants such as apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban and dabigatran. The NHS says the anticoagulant alert card should be carried at all times and shown to a doctor or dentist before any procedure. A sudden change in the amount of vitamin K in the diet can change how much warfarin a person needs.
